questions.question: What are the key differences between InnoDB and MyISAM storage engines in MySQL?
questions.title: InnoDB vs MyISAM Storage Engines
questions.direct_answer: InnoDB is the default MySQL engine offering ACID transactions, foreign keys, row-level locking, and crash recovery. MyISAM is an older engine with faster read performance for non-transactional workloads but lacks transactions, foreign key support, and uses table-level locking. For most modern Java/Spring Boot applications, InnoDB is the correct choice.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests understanding of MySQL internals, when to choose the right storage engine, and awareness of transactional guarantees critical for production Java applications.

sections.title: InnoDB vs MyISAM — Why It Matters
sections.content: MySQL supports multiple storage engines that handle how data is physically stored and retrieved. The two most historically significant are InnoDB (default since MySQL 5.5) and MyISAM (legacy default). Choosing the wrong engine can lead to data corruption, poor concurrency, or missing constraint enforcement in your Spring Boot application.

sections.title: InnoDB vs MyISAM Feature Comparison
sections.caption: InnoDB vs MyISAM Feature Comparison
sections.content:
### InnoDB vs MyISAM Feature Comparison

| Feature | InnoDB | MyISAM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ACID Transactions | ✅ Full support | ❌ Not supported |
| Foreign Keys | ✅ Enforced | ❌ Ignored |
| Locking Granularity | ✅ Row-level | ⚠️ Table-level |
| Crash Recovery | ✅ Automatic via redo log | ❌ Manual repair needed |
| Full-Text Search | ✅ Since MySQL 5.6 | ✅ Native support |
| Read Performance (no concurrency) | ⚠️ Slightly slower | ✅ Faster |
| Write Concurrency | ✅ High (row locks) | ❌ Low (table locks) |
| MVCC | ✅ Supported | ❌ Not supported |
| Spring/JPA Compatibility | ✅ Full | ⚠️ Partial (no rollback) |
| Compressed Tables | ✅ Supported | ⚠️ Limited |

sections.title: Production notes
sections.content:
### Operational checklist for Spring Boot + InnoDB

When you scaffold entities with JPA, confirm migrations explicitly set `ENGINE=InnoDB` (some older templates still omitted it). In production, pair transactional services with InnoDB so retry policies and outbox patterns actually mean something: a rolled-back service method should leave no persisted rows, which MyISAM cannot guarantee. If you inherit MyISAM tables, plan a low-risk migration window: `ALTER TABLE ... ENGINE=InnoDB` copies the table—test duration on a clone first, watch disk space, and temporarily cap application concurrency while the DDL runs. Finally, teach junior developers that “storage engine” is not cosmetic: it changes locking, backups, and replication behavior under failure.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **InnoDB: row-level locking vs MyISAM table-level locking** — a MyISAM UPDATE blocks every concurrent write on the entire table; an InnoDB UPDATE blocks only rows with conflicting keys
- **InnoDB: ACID transactions; MyISAM: none** — MyISAM has no rollback; a crashed multi-statement operation leaves data in a partially written state with no recovery path
- **InnoDB enforces foreign keys; MyISAM parses but ignores them** — declaring a FK on a MyISAM table compiles without error but never enforces referential integrity at runtime
- **InnoDB full-text search since MySQL 5.6** — the last practical reason to use MyISAM is gone; FULLTEXT indexes work on InnoDB tables in all modern MySQL versions
- **ALTER TABLE t ENGINE=InnoDB migrates MyISAM tables** — rebuilds the table with full InnoDB capabilities; required before enabling FK constraints or transactions on legacy tables

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
InnoDB and MyISAM are the two MySQL storage engines that come up most in interviews — InnoDB has been the default since MySQL 5.5 and the right choice for virtually every modern application.

**InnoDB — the default for good reason**
- InnoDB supports full ACID transactions, which means a multi-statement operation like debit account A and credit account B either both succeed or both roll back on crash — something MyISAM simply cannot do
- Row-level locking means concurrent writers block each other only when they touch the same row; MyISAM uses table-level locking, which means a single UPDATE blocks every other write on the table
- InnoDB enforces foreign key constraints at the database level, which means referential integrity is guaranteed even if the application has a bug; MyISAM ignores foreign key declarations entirely

**MyISAM — where it still exists**
- MyISAM was the historical default before MySQL 5.5 and is still present in legacy codebases; its main advantage was slightly faster reads on simple SELECT-heavy workloads with no concurrent writes
- Full-text search in older MySQL versions required MyISAM — but InnoDB has supported full-text indexes since MySQL 5.6, removing the last real reason to use MyISAM in new development
- If you encounter a MyISAM table in an existing system, the migration path to InnoDB is `ALTER TABLE t ENGINE=InnoDB` — it rebuilds the table with full InnoDB capabilities

For any new table in a Spring Boot application: InnoDB. The transaction and row-locking guarantees are non-negotiable for any data that matters, and full-text search, spatial queries, and all other specialized capabilities are available in InnoDB today.

questions.question: What index types does MySQL support, and when should you use B-tree, full-text, and composite indexes?
questions.title: MySQL Index Types: B-tree, Full-text, and Composite
questions.direct_answer: MySQL supports B-tree (default), Hash, Full-text, and Spatial indexes. B-tree indexes power most range queries and equality lookups. Full-text indexes handle natural language search across text columns. Composite indexes (multi-column B-tree) accelerate queries filtering on multiple columns, following the leftmost prefix rule.
questions.interviewer_intent: Assesses knowledge of query optimization fundamentals. Interviewers want to know whether the candidate understands index selection, the leftmost prefix rule, and how Spring Data JPA queries interact with indexes.

sections.title: The Index Landscape in MySQL
sections.content: Indexes in MySQL are data structures that allow the database engine to find rows without scanning the entire table. Choosing the right index type and understanding how MySQL uses them is one of the most impactful performance skills for a backend Java developer. Poorly indexed tables are the most common cause of slow queries in Spring Boot applications.

sections.title: Creating and Using Different MySQL Index Types
sections.caption: Creating and using different MySQL index types

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Composite left-prefix rule in MySQL** — `(status, created_at)` cannot serve `WHERE created_at > ?` alone; the leading column must appear in the filter, or MySQL falls back to a full scan
- **InnoDB primary key is the clustered index** — all data rows live in primary key order; secondary indexes include the PK as a suffix, which means range scans on the PK are naturally fast
- **FULLTEXT replaces LIKE '%term%'** — `MATCH ... AGAINST` uses an inverted index; `LIKE '%spring%'` cannot use any index and scans every row; FULLTEXT is available on InnoDB since MySQL 5.6
- **Covering index eliminates heap reads** — when all columns in SELECT and WHERE are in the index, MySQL reads only the index leaf pages; `Extra: Using index` in EXPLAIN confirms this
- **`EXPLAIN` must confirm index usage** — the optimizer may ignore an index if statistics are stale or the table is small; always verify the key column in EXPLAIN output

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MySQL supports several index types, but B-tree covers the vast majority of production query patterns. Understanding when other index types apply — and how composite index design works — is what actually moves query performance.

**B-tree — the universal default**
- B-tree keeps index values in sorted order, which means it handles equality (`=`), ranges (`BETWEEN`, `>`, `<`), and `ORDER BY` all in one structure — O(log n) traversal to find the starting entry, then a sequential scan along the leaf pages for ranges
- When you run `CREATE INDEX` without specifying a type, MySQL creates a B-tree; InnoDB also uses B-tree for its clustered primary key, which means secondary indexes always include the primary key as a hidden suffix

**Composite indexes — design around your queries**
- An index on `(status, created_at)` serves `WHERE status = ? AND created_at > ?` efficiently, but not `WHERE created_at > ?` alone — because the leading `status` column must be present to establish a starting position in the sorted index
- The most selective equality filter should lead; range conditions go last; columns only in SELECT can be added with `INCLUDE` (MySQL 8.0.13+) for covering index behavior

**FULLTEXT — for natural language search**
- FULLTEXT indexes tokenize and index words, which means `MATCH(body) AGAINST('spring boot')` finds documents containing those terms without a full-table scan or `LIKE '%spring%'` which can't use any index
- Available on InnoDB since MySQL 5.6; supports boolean mode (`+spring -python`) and natural language mode with relevance scoring

**Spatial and Hash**
- Spatial (R-tree) indexes support geometric queries — finding all locations within a bounding box; used with MySQL's geometry data types
- Hash indexes exist only in the MEMORY engine; InnoDB's adaptive hash index is internal and automatic, not user-created

Always validate with `EXPLAIN` that MySQL actually uses the index you expect — the optimizer sometimes prefers a full table scan when the table is small or statistics are stale.

questions.question: How do you use MySQL EXPLAIN to identify and fix slow queries in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Using EXPLAIN to Optimize MySQL Queries
questions.direct_answer: EXPLAIN shows the query execution plan: which indexes MySQL uses, the join type, estimated rows scanned, and whether a filesort or temporary table is needed. You look for 'ALL' in the type column (full table scan), NULL in the key column (no index used), and high rows estimates — then add appropriate indexes or rewrite the query to fix them.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests practical query tuning skill. Interviewers want to see that the candidate can read an EXPLAIN output, identify bottlenecks, and know the remediation steps rather than just theoretically knowing indexes exist.

sections.title: Why EXPLAIN Is Your Best Friend in Production
sections.content: EXPLAIN (and its more detailed variant EXPLAIN ANALYZE in MySQL 8.0+) reveals how the MySQL query optimizer plans to execute your query. Every senior Java/Spring Boot developer should be comfortable reading EXPLAIN output, because mismatched or missing indexes are the #1 cause of production performance degradation. The key columns to focus on are: type, key, rows, and Extra.

sections.title: Reading EXPLAIN Output and Fixing a Slow Query
sections.caption: Reading EXPLAIN output and fixing a slow query
sections.annotated_code:
-- STEP 1: Run EXPLAIN on a slow query
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND created_at > '2024-01-01';

-- Typical bad output (no index on status/created_at):
-- +----+-------------+--------+------+------+------+-------+
-- | id | select_type | table  | type | key  | rows | Extra |
-- +----+-------------+--------+------+------+------+-------+
-- | 1  | SIMPLE      | orders | ALL  | NULL | 5000 | Using where |
-- ^^^ type=ALL means full table scan — BAD for large tables
-- ^^^ key=NULL means no index used
-- ^^^ rows=5000 means MySQL estimates scanning all rows

-- STEP 2: Add a composite index covering both filter columns
CREATE INDEX idx_status_created ON orders(status, created_at);

-- STEP 3: Re-run EXPLAIN to confirm index is used
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND created_at > '2024-01-01';
-- +----+-------------+--------+-------+--------------------+------+
-- | id | select_type | table  | type  | key                | rows |
-- +----+-------------+--------+-------+--------------------+------+
-- | 1  | SIMPLE      | orders | range | idx_status_created | 12   |
-- ^^^ type=range is good — only scans matching range
-- ^^^ key=idx_status_created — index is now being used
-- ^^^ rows=12 — down from 5000, much better!

-- STEP 4: MySQL 8.0+ — use EXPLAIN ANALYZE for actual runtimes
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING' AND created_at > '2024-01-01';
-- Returns actual vs estimated rows and actual execution time per node

-- EXTRA column warning signs:
-- 'Using filesort'    → ORDER BY can't use an index, costly sort in memory/disk
-- 'Using temporary'  → GROUP BY or UNION forced a temp table
-- 'Using index'      → Good! Covering index, no row lookup needed
-- 'Using where'      → Filter applied after index lookup (normal)

-- STEP 5: Enable slow query log in Spring Boot application.properties
-- spring.datasource.hikari.connection-init-sql=SET SESSION long_query_time=1
-- Or in MySQL: SET GLOBAL slow_query_log = 'ON'; SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 1;

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`type: ALL` = full table scan** — every row is read regardless of WHERE; the most urgent optimization signal; look for a missing or unused index on the filter column
- **`key: NULL` when an index exists** — the optimizer chose a scan over the index; usually caused by stale statistics (`ANALYZE TABLE`) or low selectivity on the indexed column
- **`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows actual vs estimated rows** — MySQL 8.0+ only; runs the query and surfaces cases where the cost model is wrong, preventing optimization based on misleading estimates
- **`Extra: Using filesort`** — ORDER BY could not use an index; MySQL sorts in memory or on disk; add the ORDER BY column(s) to the index to eliminate the sort pass
- **`Extra: Using index`** — covering index in use; the table is never read; the ideal result for a read-heavy query where index design matches the SELECT and WHERE columns

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When a MySQL query is slow, `EXPLAIN` is the first tool to use — it shows exactly how MySQL plans to execute the query: which indexes it considers, which it picks, and how many rows it expects to scan.

**Reading the key columns**
- `type` is the most important column — `ALL` means a full table scan reading every row; `ref` or `eq_ref` means an index lookup; `range` means an index range scan; ideally you want anything other than `ALL` on large tables
- `key` shows which index MySQL actually chose — if it's NULL when you expected an index, the optimizer decided the scan was cheaper, often because statistics are stale or the selectivity is low
- `rows` is the estimated rows MySQL expects to examine — a mismatch between `rows` and the actual result count is a signal that `ANALYZE TABLE` is needed to refresh statistics

**EXPLAIN ANALYZE — actual vs estimated**
- MySQL 8.0 added `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` which actually executes the query and shows actual row counts and execution times alongside the estimates — this is the tool that surfaces cases where the planner's cost model is wrong
- Look for large gaps between estimated and actual rows — if estimated=100 but actual=50,000, the index choice was based on wrong data; running `ANALYZE TABLE` updates the statistics the optimizer uses

**Extra column — what to watch for**
- `Using filesort` means MySQL couldn't satisfy `ORDER BY` with the index, which means an additional sort pass runs in memory or on disk — adding the ORDER BY columns to the index eliminates it
- `Using temporary` means MySQL created an internal temp table — common with GROUP BY on non-indexed columns; adding an index on the GROUP BY column can eliminate it
- `Using index` means a covering index is being used — all columns needed are in the index and the table itself is not read; the best possible extra value for a read query

questions.question: What are MySQL transaction isolation levels and how do they affect concurrency in Spring Boot applications?
questions.title: MySQL Transaction Isolation Levels
questions.direct_answer: MySQL InnoDB supports four isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ (default), and SERIALIZABLE. Higher isolation prevents more concurrency anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantom reads) but reduces throughput. Spring Boot's @Transactional annotation lets you configure isolation per method.
questions.interviewer_intent: Assesses deep understanding of database concurrency. Interviewers want to know whether the candidate can reason about data consistency vs. performance trade-offs and configure Spring @Transactional correctly for their use case.

sections.title: The Concurrency vs Consistency Trade-off
sections.content: Transaction isolation defines how changes made by one transaction are visible to other concurrent transactions. The SQL standard defines three anomalies that isolation levels protect against: dirty reads (seeing uncommitted data), non-repeatable reads (same query returns different results in same transaction), and phantom reads (new rows appear in a repeated range query). MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, which uses MVCC to prevent most anomalies without full serialization.

sections.title: MySQL Isolation Levels vs Concurrency Anomalies
sections.caption: MySQL Isolation Levels vs. Concurrency Anomalies
sections.footnote: * InnoDB REPEATABLE READ prevents phantom reads for snapshot reads (SELECT) via MVCC, but current reads (SELECT FOR UPDATE) can still see phantoms without gap locks.
sections.content:
### MySQL Isolation Levels vs. Concurrency Anomalies

| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Non-repeatable Read | Phantom Read | Spring Isolation Constant |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| READ UNCOMMITTED | ❌ Possible | ❌ Possible | ❌ Possible | Isolation.READ_UNCOMMITTED |
| READ COMMITTED | ✅ Prevented | ❌ Possible | ❌ Possible | Isolation.READ_COMMITTED |
| REPEATABLE READ (default) | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ⚠️ Partially prevented* | Isolation.REPEATABLE_READ |
| SERIALIZABLE | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | ✅ Prevented | Isolation.SERIALIZABLE |

* InnoDB REPEATABLE READ prevents phantom reads for snapshot reads (SELECT) via MVCC, but current reads (SELECT FOR UPDATE) can still see phantoms without gap locks.

sections.title: Production notes
sections.content:
### How Spring developers feel isolation in real APIs

A common pattern is a read-modify-write flow: load an aggregate, apply business rules, save. Under `READ COMMITTED`, another transaction can change rows between your SELECT and UPDATE, so you may need optimistic locking (`@Version`) or targeted `SELECT FOR UPDATE` anyway. Under InnoDB’s default `REPEATABLE READ`, consistent reads see a stable snapshot for plain SELECTs, which simplifies many report-style transactions but still interacts with write locks on updates. For financial ledgers or inventory, interviewers often expect you to mention that application-level invariants may still require idempotency keys and careful transaction boundaries even when the database isolation level is strong.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **MySQL defaults to Repeatable Read; PostgreSQL defaults to Read Committed** — the same application running on both databases may behave differently under concurrent load without explicit isolation level settings
- **Repeatable Read uses MVCC for consistent snapshots** — InnoDB takes a snapshot at transaction start; reads within the transaction always see that snapshot, avoiding read locks on rows being read
- **Gap locks under Repeatable Read cause deadlocks** — `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a range locks the gap; two transactions locking overlapping ranges and then inserting deadlock against each other; switch to Read Committed for insert-heavy workloads
- **`SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL` is per-session** — changes the current session only; the global default is set in `my.cnf` via `transaction-isolation`
- **Serializable prevents phantom reads via predicate locks** — required when a transaction must guarantee that a range scan returns the same rows on second read; adds significant lock contention for concurrent writers

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MySQL uses Repeatable Read as its default isolation level — different from PostgreSQL which defaults to Read Committed. That difference matters when porting code between databases or diagnosing unexpected query behavior.

**The four levels and what they prevent**
- Read Uncommitted allows dirty reads — your transaction can see another transaction's uncommitted changes, which means you might read data that gets rolled back; almost never appropriate
- Read Committed prevents dirty reads — you only see committed data, but two reads of the same row in one transaction can return different values if another transaction commits between them (non-repeatable read)
- Repeatable Read (MySQL default) holds a consistent snapshot from the start of the transaction — the same row returns the same value no matter how many times you read it within one transaction; InnoDB's MVCC makes this efficient without actually locking reads
- Serializable adds predicate locks, preventing phantom rows — new rows inserted by other transactions won't appear in repeated range queries; the safest but highest contention

**MySQL's Repeatable Read and gap locks**
- Under Repeatable Read, InnoDB uses gap locks to prevent phantom inserts into the range you've read — which means `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a range prevents concurrent inserts into that range, even if no rows match
- This is the source of many unexpected deadlocks in Spring Boot applications where two transactions both lock ranges and then try to insert into them

**When to change the isolation level**
- Read Committed is often sufficient for reporting queries — it avoids the gap lock overhead and is fine for analytics where phantom reads don't matter
- Serializable is rarely needed in web applications; most correctness requirements are covered by Repeatable Read plus application-level optimistic locking

questions.question: Explain InnoDB locking mechanisms: row locks, gap locks, and next-key locks. When does each apply?
questions.title: InnoDB Locking: Row Lock, Gap Lock, and Next-Key Lock
questions.direct_answer: InnoDB uses three lock granularities: row locks protect individual rows, gap locks protect the space between index values to prevent phantom inserts, and next-key locks (the default) combine both to lock a row plus the gap before it. Next-key locks are InnoDB's primary mechanism for preventing phantom reads under REPEATABLE READ without full SERIALIZABLE isolation.

sections.title: How InnoDB Locking Actually Works
sections.content: InnoDB implements row-level locking via its index-based lock system. All locks are attached to index entries, not physical rows. Understanding lock types is essential for diagnosing deadlocks in Spring Boot applications — the most common production incident caused by database concurrency issues. InnoDB automatically uses the appropriate lock type depending on the query, the isolation level, and whether the query is a snapshot read or a current (locking) read.

sections.title: InnoDB Lock Types in Practice
sections.caption: Demonstrating InnoDB lock types with practical examples
sections.code:
-- Setup: orders table with an index on status
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  status VARCHAR(20),
  total  DECIMAL(10,2),
  INDEX  idx_status (status)
);
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,'PENDING',100),(5,'PENDING',200),(10,'DONE',50);

-- 1. ROW LOCK: locks the exact index record
--    Acquired by SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a unique index hit
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 5 FOR UPDATE;
-- Locks only the row with id=5. Other transactions can still
-- read/write id=1 or id=10 concurrently.

-- 2. GAP LOCK: locks the gap BETWEEN index values, prevents inserts
--    Acquired when searching a range on a non-unique index
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = 'PENDING' FOR UPDATE;
-- Locks the gap before the first PENDING row and after the last PENDING row.
-- Another transaction CANNOT insert a new PENDING order until this commits.
-- Gap locks are SHARED — two transactions can both hold gap locks on same gap.

-- 3. NEXT-KEY LOCK: row lock + gap lock before it (default InnoDB lock)
--    Used for range scans to prevent phantoms
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id BETWEEN 3 AND 8 FOR UPDATE;
-- Acquires next-key lock on (id=5 row) + gap (1, 5] + gap (5, 10)
-- Prevents: insert of id=4, id=6, id=7, or id=8 by other transactions

-- DIAGNOSING DEADLOCKS in Spring Boot:
-- InnoDB rolls back the lighter transaction and throws:
-- com.mysql.cj.jdbc.exceptions.MySQLTransactionRollbackException
-- (mapped to Spring's CannotAcquireLockException)

-- Check the latest deadlock details:
SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS;
-- Look for 'LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK' section

-- Avoid deadlocks: always acquire locks in the same order across transactions
-- Use @Retryable in Spring to retry on CannotAcquireLockException

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **InnoDB locks index entries, not physical rows** — a query on an unindexed column must lock every row's index entry it examines; always filter on indexed columns to minimize lock scope
- **Gap locks prevent inserts into locked ranges** — `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a range holds gap locks; concurrent inserts into that range block; only active under Repeatable Read
- **Switching to Read Committed eliminates gap locks** — reduces deadlock frequency for insert-heavy workloads at the cost of allowing phantom reads in range scans
- **`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` vs `SELECT ... FOR SHARE`** — FOR UPDATE locks exclusively (blocks reads and writes); FOR SHARE locks shared (allows reads, blocks writes); use FOR SHARE when you only need to prevent modification, not concurrent reads
- **`SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS` shows deadlock details** — the output lists the exact locks held and waited on by each deadlocked transaction; read it before guessing at the cause

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
InnoDB's locking system is more complex than most developers expect because locks don't attach to rows — they attach to index entries. That distinction is the root cause of most unexpected deadlock and blocking behaviors in Spring Boot applications.

**Row locks — locking index entries**
- InnoDB row locks are placed on index entries, not physical rows — which means if a query filters on an unindexed column, InnoDB must examine all rows and lock the entire table's index entries to guarantee no matching row is modified concurrently
- Always filter on indexed columns in `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` and `UPDATE WHERE` — queries that fall back to table scans hold far more locks than necessary

**Gap locks — protecting ranges**
- A gap lock prevents other transactions from inserting into the gap between two existing index values — so `SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id BETWEEN 10 AND 20 FOR UPDATE` locks not just rows 10-20, but the gaps between them, preventing any insert of id 11-19 from another transaction
- Gap locks only exist under Repeatable Read; switching to Read Committed eliminates them, which reduces deadlock frequency in insert-heavy workloads

**Next-key locks — the combination**
- A next-key lock is a row lock plus a gap lock on the preceding gap — InnoDB's default locking mode under Repeatable Read combines both to prevent both row modification and phantom inserts in a scanned range
- This is why two transactions that read the same range and then insert into it deadlock: each holds a gap lock the other needs for its insert

When you see deadlocks in production, check `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS` — the output shows the exact locks held and waited on by each transaction in the deadlock cycle.

questions.question: How does MySQL primary-replica replication work and how does it affect a Spring Boot application's read/write strategy?
questions.title: MySQL Replication: Primary-Replica Setup
questions.direct_answer: MySQL replication streams binary log (binlog) events from the primary to one or more replicas asynchronously. The replica's I/O thread fetches binlog events, and the SQL thread replays them. In Spring Boot, you configure separate DataSource beans for reads (replica) and writes (primary) using AbstractRoutingDataSource to distribute load and scale reads horizontally.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests architecture awareness and ability to design scalable database layers. Interviewers want to see that the candidate understands replication lag, read-after-write consistency risks, and how to handle them in Spring Boot.

sections.title: How MySQL Replication Scales Reads
sections.content: MySQL replication allows one primary (master) node to replicate all writes to one or more replica (slave) nodes. The primary writes changes to its binary log; each replica connects, downloads binlog events, and applies them in sequence. This enables read scaling (route SELECT queries to replicas), high availability (replica can be promoted if primary fails), and backups without impacting the primary. The critical gotcha is replication lag: replicas may be seconds behind the primary, causing stale reads after a write.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Async replication allows data loss on primary crash** — the primary commits and acknowledges before any replica confirms receipt; semi-sync replication eliminates this window at the cost of write latency
- **Replication lag breaks read-your-writes** — a user reads from a lagging replica immediately after writing and sees the old value; route reads to the primary for a short post-write window to guarantee consistency
- **Row-based replication (binlog_format=ROW) is safer than statement-based** — replicates exact row changes; statement-based replication breaks for non-deterministic functions like `NOW()` or `RAND()`
- **`SHOW REPLICA STATUS`** — shows `Seconds_Behind_Source` (replica lag) and any SQL/IO thread errors; the first monitoring check for replication problems
- **GTID-based replication simplifies failover** — Global Transaction IDs make it possible to promote any replica to primary without manually calculating binlog position; strongly recommended for new setups

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MySQL primary-replica replication is the standard way to scale reads — the primary handles all writes and streams those changes to one or more replicas via the binary log.

**How it works**
- Every write on the primary is recorded in the binary log (binlog) in the order it commits — each replica runs an I/O thread that connects to the primary and copies the binlog, then an SQL thread that replays those events on the replica's local data
- The replica applies events asynchronously by default, which means there's always some replication lag — how much depends on the replica's hardware and how fast the primary is generating writes

**Asynchronous vs semi-synchronous replication**
- With default async replication, a primary acknowledges a commit before any replica confirms receipt — which means a primary crash can lose committed transactions that hadn't yet been streamed to replicas
- Semi-synchronous replication (`rpl_semi_sync_master_enabled`) waits for at least one replica to acknowledge receiving the binlog before the primary acknowledges the commit — this reduces the data loss window at the cost of slightly higher write latency

**Replication lag and read-your-writes**
- Replication lag means a read replica may return stale data — a user who just submitted a form may not see their change on the next page load if the read goes to a lagging replica
- The Spring Boot solution: use `@Primary` or a separate DataSource for writes, and route reads to replicas; implement read-your-writes by routing reads to the primary for a short window after a write, or using `WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET` to wait for the replica to catch up

Row-based replication (binlog_format=ROW) replicates the exact row changes rather than the SQL statements, which makes replication deterministic for non-deterministic functions like `NOW()` and avoids many replication consistency issues.

questions.question: What is MySQL table partitioning and when should you use it in a Java backend application?
questions.title: Partitioning in MySQL
questions.direct_answer: MySQL partitioning splits a large table into smaller physical sub-tables while presenting a single logical table to the application. The four main types are RANGE (split by value range, e.g., date), LIST (split by explicit values), HASH (even distribution), and KEY (similar to HASH using MySQL's own hash). Partitioning helps prune scans on large time-series or event tables but is not a substitute for proper indexing.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests knowledge of advanced MySQL features for managing large tables. Interviewers want to know whether the candidate understands partition pruning, its limitations with foreign keys, and whether they would reach for partitioning vs. sharding vs. archiving for a given scale problem.

sections.title: When Indexes Aren't Enough — Enter Partitioning
sections.content: When a MySQL table grows into the tens or hundreds of millions of rows, even well-indexed queries can become slow because index scans still touch too many leaf pages. Partitioning addresses this by dividing the table's data files by a partition key — if a query's WHERE clause includes that key, MySQL can skip entire partitions (partition pruning), making the effective table size much smaller. Common use cases in Java backends include audit logs, time-series events, and order history tables.

sections.title: RANGE Partitioning by Date — Events Table
sections.caption: MySQL RANGE partitioning on a date column — events table
sections.code:
-- RANGE partitioning: rows assigned to partitions by year
CREATE TABLE events (
  id         BIGINT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  user_id    INT NOT NULL,
  event_type VARCHAR(50),
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL,
  payload    JSON,
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)  -- partition key MUST be in PK for InnoDB
)
PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(created_at)) (
  PARTITION p2022 VALUES LESS THAN (2023),
  PARTITION p2023 VALUES LESS THAN (2024),
  PARTITION p2024 VALUES LESS THAN (2025),
  PARTITION p2025 VALUES LESS THAN (2026),
  PARTITION p_future VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE
);

-- Partition pruning in action:
-- This query only scans p2024, skipping all other partitions
SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31';

-- Verify pruning with EXPLAIN PARTITIONS
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at >= '2024-06-01';
-- partitions column shows only: p2024,p2025,p_future  (not p2022, p2023)

-- Drop old data efficiently: just drop the partition (instant DDL)
ALTER TABLE events DROP PARTITION p2022;
-- vs: DELETE FROM events WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2022  (slow, locks table)

-- Add a new partition before p_future fills up:
ALTER TABLE events REORGANIZE PARTITION p_future INTO (
  PARTITION p2026 VALUES LESS THAN (2027),
  PARTITION p_future VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE
);

-- LIMITATION: InnoDB partitioned tables CANNOT have foreign keys
-- Spring Boot JPA: use @CreationTimestamp on created_at to ensure it's always set

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Partition pruning requires the partition key in WHERE** — a query without the partition column in its filter scans all partitions, which is worse than a regular full table scan; partition-key-less queries defeat the entire purpose
- **RANGE partitioning on date columns is the most useful pattern** — queries bounded by a date range prune irrelevant partitions automatically; archiving drops an entire partition in milliseconds instead of deleting millions of rows
- **`ALTER TABLE t DROP PARTITION` is instant for archiving** — removes a partition's data file directly; equivalent to `DELETE WHERE created_at < ?` but without generating per-row binlog events or holding locks
- **Foreign keys are not supported on partitioned tables** — a hard MySQL limitation; referential integrity must be enforced at the application layer for partitioned tables
- **Hash partitioning does not help read pruning** — rows are distributed by hash for write balance; queries cannot predict which partition a hash value lands in, so all partitions are scanned

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MySQL partitioning splits a large table into smaller physical segments while presenting them as one logical table. It's most effective for time-series data where queries are naturally bounded by a date range.

**How partitioning helps**
- When a query includes the partition key in the WHERE clause, MySQL's query optimizer performs partition pruning — it reads only the relevant partitions, which means a query for last month's data scans one partition instead of scanning the entire 10-billion-row table
- This also makes archiving old data fast: dropping a range partition (`ALTER TABLE t DROP PARTITION p2022`) removes an entire month of data in milliseconds, much faster than `DELETE WHERE created_at < '2023-01-01'` which generates binlog events for every row

**Partition types**
- RANGE partitioning on a date or integer column is the most common — `PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(created_at))` creates separate segments per year, and partition pruning eliminates years the query doesn't need
- LIST partitioning works on discrete values — `PARTITION BY LIST (region_id)` — useful for multi-tenant data where queries are always scoped to one region
- HASH and KEY partitioning distribute rows evenly by hash — useful for write distribution across multiple tablespaces, less useful for query pruning

**What partitioning doesn't fix**
- Queries that don't include the partition key in WHERE have no pruning — they scan all partitions, which is often slower than an equivalent full table scan due to per-partition overhead
- Foreign keys are not supported on partitioned tables in MySQL — a significant limitation for schemas with referential integrity

Consider partitioning when a table has hundreds of millions of rows, queries are consistently range-bounded by a high-cardinality date or integer column, and archiving old data is a regular operation.

questions.question: How does MySQL query caching work and what are the modern best practices for query optimization in MySQL 8.0?
questions.title: MySQL Query Cache and Query Optimization
questions.direct_answer: MySQL's built-in query cache was removed in MySQL 8.0 because it caused severe mutex contention under concurrent write workloads. Modern query-level caching should be handled at the application layer using Redis or Caffeine in Spring Boot. Query optimization in MySQL 8.0 instead focuses on the improved cost-based optimizer, invisible indexes, descending indexes, and histogram statistics.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests whether candidates have current MySQL 8.0 knowledge and can distinguish between database-level and application-level caching strategies. Shows awareness of why naively relying on MySQL's old query cache was an anti-pattern.

sections.title: Why MySQL Killed the Query Cache
sections.content: MySQL 5.x had a server-side query cache that stored the full result set of SELECT queries and returned cached results for identical queries. However, it used a global mutex that serialized all cache reads and invalidated the entire cache for any write to a referenced table, causing severe contention in write-heavy production systems. MySQL 8.0 removed the query cache entirely. Modern optimization relies on proper indexing, the improved cost-based optimizer, and application-layer caching in Spring Boot using Spring Cache with Redis or Caffeine.

sections.title: Application-Layer Caching in Spring Boot
sections.caption: Application-layer caching in Spring Boot to replace MySQL query cache

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **MySQL query cache removed in 8.0** — it used a global mutex that serialized all cache operations and invalidated entire table caches on any write; under concurrent workloads it degraded performance rather than improving it
- **Application-level cache (Redis) replaces it** — cache-aside with TTL gives fine-grained invalidation control and scales without a global database mutex; `@Cacheable` with Redis in Spring Boot is the standard pattern
- **`innodb_buffer_pool_size` is the real in-memory cache** — set to 70-80% of RAM on a dedicated database server; this caches InnoDB data and index pages, reducing disk I/O for hot data; more impactful than any query cache
- **`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (MySQL 8.0+) for slow query tuning** — shows actual vs estimated rows and actual execution time; use it alongside the slow query log to find and fix the real bottlenecks
- **Slow query log finds recurring offenders** — `slow_query_log=ON`, `long_query_time=1` logs queries taking over 1 second; `mysqldumpslow` or `pt-query-digest` aggregates them by query pattern

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
MySQL's built-in query cache was removed in MySQL 8.0 — and the reason is worth understanding, because it informs how you should implement caching instead.

**Why the query cache was removed**
- The MySQL query cache stored complete SELECT result sets and returned them for identical queries — but it used a single global mutex that serialized every cache lookup and invalidated the entire cache entry for a table on any write
- Under concurrent write workloads, this global mutex became a severe bottleneck: threads queued behind it even for reads on tables that hadn't changed, and every write to any row in a table invalidated all cached queries on that table regardless of whether the query touched those rows
- The result: the query cache made concurrent write-heavy applications slower than having no cache at all, which is why it was deprecated in MySQL 5.7 and removed in 8.0

**What to use instead**
- Application-level caching with Redis or Memcached is the correct replacement — it sits outside the database, doesn't hold the global mutex, and gives you control over invalidation at the granularity that makes sense for your data
- The cache-aside pattern: check Redis first, if not found query MySQL, store the result in Redis with a TTL, return; invalidate the cache key when you write to the underlying table
- MySQL 8.0 query optimization instead: use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, add covering indexes for hot queries, enable the InnoDB buffer pool to cache data pages in memory (the `innodb_buffer_pool_size` setting should be 70-80% of available RAM on a dedicated database server)

For Spring Boot, use `@Cacheable` with a Redis cache manager rather than relying on database-level caching.

questions.question: How do you tune MySQL connection pool settings in Spring Boot for production workloads?
questions.title: Spring Boot + MySQL Connection Pool Tuning
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot defaults to HikariCP as its connection pool. Key tuning parameters are maximumPoolSize (limit concurrent connections to MySQL's thread capacity), minimumIdle (warm connections for burst traffic), connectionTimeout (fail fast instead of queuing forever), and idleTimeout. For production, align maximumPoolSize with your MySQL max_connections limit divided by the number of application instances.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests practical production engineering knowledge. Interviewers want to see that the candidate has operated Spring Boot with MySQL in production, understands the HikariCP parameters, and knows how to diagnose connection pool exhaustion.

sections.title: Why Connection Pool Tuning Prevents Outages
sections.content: Spring Boot auto-configures HikariCP as its connection pool. The pool maintains a set of pre-opened database connections that are reused across requests, avoiding the overhead of opening a new TCP connection for each query. Misconfigured pool settings are a frequent cause of production outages: too few connections starve concurrent requests, too many overwhelm MySQL's thread pool and memory, and wrong timeout values can cause cascading failures under load.

sections.title: Calculate and set maximumPoolSize
sections.content:
The most critical setting. HikariCP's formula is: pool size = (core count × 2) + effective spindle count. For a typical cloud instance with 4 vCPUs and SSD storage, that is roughly 10 connections per application instance. Multiply by your application instance count and ensure it stays below MySQL's max_connections (default 151). Reserve ~20 connections for admin, monitoring, and replication threads.

```sql
# application.properties
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size=10
# For a 3-instance deployment: 3 × 10 = 30 connections to MySQL
# MySQL max_connections should be at least 50 (30 app + 20 admin overhead)

# Check MySQL's current max_connections:
# SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'max_connections';
# SET GLOBAL max_connections = 200;
```

sections.title: Configure timeouts to fail fast
sections.content:
connectionTimeout is the maximum time a thread waits for a connection from the pool before throwing an exception. Set it low (2-5 seconds) so that pool exhaustion surfaces quickly as an error rather than queuing indefinitely, which causes cascading thread starvation. idleTimeout removes idle connections after the specified duration. maxLifetime recycles connections before MySQL's wait_timeout closes them server-side.

```sql
# application.properties — production-safe timeout settings
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout=3000        # 3 seconds — fail fast
spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout=600000            # 10 minutes
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime=1800000           # 30 minutes (< MySQL wait_timeout)
spring.datasource.hikari.keepalive-time=60000           # 1 min ping to prevent stale conns

# MySQL server-side: SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'wait_timeout'; -- typically 28800s (8h)
# max-lifetime MUST be less than MySQL wait_timeout to avoid 'connection closed' errors
```

The application pool settings only work if the MySQL server is configured to support them. Set max_connections high enough to handle all your application instances plus overhead. -- MySQL server tuning for connection pool workloads
-- my.cnf / my.ini
-- [mysqld]
-- max_connections = 200
-- thread_cache_size = 16         # Reuse threads, reduces new-connection cost
-- wait_timeout = 1800            # 30 minutes — aligns with HikariCP max-lifetime
-- interactive_timeout = 1800
-- max_allowed_packet = 64M       # Increase for large JSON/blob payloads

-- Monitor connection usage:
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Threads_connected';  -- current open connections
SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Connection_errors%'; -- connection refusals

sections.content:
- **`maximumPoolSize = (cores x 2) + spindles`** — HikariCP's formula; for a 4-core MySQL server roughly 9-10 connections outperform 200 because MySQL CPU is the real bottleneck, not connection slots
- **`connectionTimeout: 3000-5000ms` for production** — the default 30s means a thread hangs 30s before discovering the pool is exhausted; 3-5s fails fast and frees server threads before the HTTP timeout fires
- **`max-lifetime` prevents `wait_timeout` disconnects** — MySQL closes idle connections after `wait_timeout` (default 8 hours); set `max-lifetime` below that value so HikariCP rotates connections before MySQL drops them
- **`hikaricp_pending_threads > 0` signals a problem** — threads queuing for a connection indicates either pool undersizing or queries holding connections for abnormally long durations; investigate slow queries first
- **Multiple DataSources need separate pool configs** — a read-write primary pool and a read-replica pool should be configured with different `maximumPoolSize` values based on their expected workload ratios

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot uses HikariCP as its default connection pool, and most connection pool problems in production come from two settings: `maximumPoolSize` and `connectionTimeout`.

**maximumPoolSize — smaller than you think**
- The common mistake is setting this to match the thread count or expected concurrent requests — but the bottleneck is the database CPU and disk, not connection slot availability
- HikariCP's own guidance: `(number of CPU cores x 2) + effective spindle count` — for a 4-core MySQL server, that's roughly 9-10 connections, not 100 or 200; a pool that's too large causes connection queuing at the MySQL layer, consuming memory without improving throughput
- Monitor `hikaricp_pending_threads` — if threads are consistently waiting for a connection, either the pool is undersized or queries are holding connections too long

**connectionTimeout — fail fast**
- `connectionTimeout` controls how long a thread waits for a pool connection before throwing `SQLTimeoutException` — the Spring Boot default is 30 seconds, which is far too long for production; a user's HTTP request will have timed out before that
- Set it to 3-5 seconds so that when the pool is exhausted, callers fail fast rather than hanging and consuming server threads

**Key properties in application.properties**
- `spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size`: the upper connection limit
- `spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout`: milliseconds to wait for a connection (default 30000; set to 3000-5000)
- `spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout`: how long an idle connection can stay in the pool before being retired (default 600000ms)
- `spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime`: maximum connection age before rotation (default 1800000ms; prevents stale connections after MySQL's `wait_timeout` closes them)

Enable HikariCP metrics with Micrometer by adding `spring-boot-starter-actuator` — pool wait time, active connections, and pending threads are the metrics to monitor.

questions.question: How do MySQL and PostgreSQL compare for Java backend developers, and when would you choose one over the other?
questions.title: MySQL vs PostgreSQL for Java Developers
questions.direct_answer: MySQL and PostgreSQL are both excellent relational databases fully supported by Spring Data JPA and Hibernate. PostgreSQL leads on SQL standards compliance, advanced data types (JSONB, arrays, ranges), window functions, and extensibility. MySQL leads on read replication ease, widespread hosting support, and marginally simpler operational overhead for standard CRUD workloads. The choice depends on query complexity, cloud environment, and team familiarity.
questions.interviewer_intent: Tests breadth of database knowledge and ability to make pragmatic technology choices. Interviewers want to hear trade-off reasoning, not just a preference. Shows whether the candidate has worked with both databases in production Java contexts.

sections.title: Two Great Databases — Different Sweet Spots
sections.content: MySQL and PostgreSQL are both mature, open-source relational databases with full ACID compliance and excellent Spring Boot/JPA/Hibernate support. Their differences matter most at the edges: complex queries, advanced data types, replication architecture, and strict SQL standards compliance. For a standard Spring Boot CRUD application, both work equally well and switching between them requires only a dependency change and dialect update in Spring Boot.

### MySQL vs PostgreSQL — Java Developer Perspective

| Feature | MySQL 8.0 | PostgreSQL 16 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SQL Standards Compliance | ⚠️ Good, some deviations | ✅ Excellent, most compliant |
| JSON Support | ⚠️ JSON (no indexing on paths) | ✅ JSONB (indexed, operators) |
| Window Functions | ✅ Supported (8.0+) | ✅ Supported, more complete |
| CTEs (WITH clause) | ✅ Supported (8.0+) | ✅ Supported, WITH RECURSIVE |
| Full-Text Search | ⚠️ Basic built-in | ✅ Advanced with tsvector/tsquery |
| Read Replication | ✅ Simple binlog replication | ⚠️ More complex WAL streaming |
| Horizontal Sharding | ⚠️ Needs Vitess/ProxySQL | ⚠️ Needs Citus extension |
| Spring Boot Dialect | ✅ MySQLDialect | ✅ PostgreSQLDialect |
| Cloud Managed Options | ✅ RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL | ✅ RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, Supabase |
| Schema Migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) | ✅ Full support | ✅ Full support |
| Array / Range Types | ❌ Not supported | ✅ Native array, range, hstore |
| Transactional DDL | ❌ DDL auto-commits | ✅ DDL in transactions (rollback on fail) |
| Default Port | 3306 | 5432 |

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **PostgreSQL JSONB with GIN index vs MySQL JSON** — PostgreSQL allows `WHERE data @> '{"status": "active"}'` to use a GIN index; MySQL JSON queries have more limited index support and require generated column indexes for performance
- **MySQL Repeatable Read uses gap locks; PostgreSQL uses MVCC** — gap locks in MySQL under the default isolation level cause more deadlocks in concurrent insert workloads; PostgreSQL's MVCC approach avoids them
- **PostgreSQL: arrays, ranges, enums as native types** — MySQL requires workaround tables or JSON for the same data; PostgreSQL's richer type system reduces schema complexity for certain domains
- **Hibernate dialect is the only Spring Boot change** — `org.hibernate.dialect.MySQLDialect` vs `PostgreSQLDialect`; JPA queries, `@Transactional`, and Spring Data repositories behave identically on both
- **Aurora MySQL and RDS MySQL are more mature managed offerings** — for teams deploying on AWS who need managed replication and failover, MySQL's managed ecosystem is broader; Aurora PostgreSQL has caught up but MySQL is more commonly chosen for simpler operational reasons

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
For a standard Spring Boot CRUD application, MySQL and PostgreSQL are largely interchangeable at the surface — you swap the JDBC driver and Hibernate dialect and most applications work unchanged. The differences emerge at the edges.

**Where PostgreSQL has a clear advantage**
- PostgreSQL's type system is richer — JSONB with GIN indexing allows complex JSON queries at near-relational speed, whereas MySQL's JSON support has more limited indexing options; arrays and range types are native in PostgreSQL, requiring workarounds in MySQL
- PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read prevents phantom reads via MVCC without gap locks — MySQL's Repeatable Read uses gap locks under Repeatable Read, which causes more deadlocks in insert-heavy workloads
- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` in PostgreSQL shows actual vs estimated rows, actual time, and buffer hits; MySQL 8.0 added EXPLAIN ANALYZE but PostgreSQL's planner output is generally more detailed

**Where MySQL has a clear advantage**
- MySQL's ecosystem and tooling are more widely deployed — RDS, Aurora, and managed MySQL are ubiquitous; many teams have more operational experience with MySQL, which matters more than feature differences for standard workloads
- MySQL's replication is simpler to configure for basic primary-replica setups; Aurora MySQL with failover is more mature than Aurora PostgreSQL in some managed environments
- Full-text search is easier to enable on MySQL InnoDB tables for basic search needs, though Elasticsearch or PostgreSQL's full-text capabilities often replace it at scale

**For Spring Boot specifically**
- Hibernate works identically on both — dialect selection is the only difference in `application.properties`; JPA queries, `@Transactional`, and Spring Data repositories behave the same
- MySQL autocommit defaults mean each statement outside an explicit transaction is committed immediately; ensure `@Transactional` is applied wherever multiple operations must be atomic

For a standard Spring Boot CRUD application, both work equally well and switching between them requires only a dependency change and dialect update.
